source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Pseudo-count from a density model (CTS) gives a bonus that turns a DQN into an explorer on sparse-reward Atari games.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: agent consistently passes 15 of 24 rooms within 50M frames; one run reached 6600 points by 100M frames. Averages over 5 trials. Bonus scale 0.05 chosen from a coarse sweep.
limits: Gain relies on mixing the Monte Carlo return into the Double-Q target. Headline is one game and 5 trials.
agent_relevance: S3 should keep a visit count over directions tried and give a bonus to rarely tried ones.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation (A3C+, 60 games)
finding: Across 60 Atari games the bonus helps actor-critic modestly, mostly where plain exploration fails.
numbers: A3C fails (not 50% above random) in 15 games; A3C+ fails in 10, of which 8 are games where DQN also fails. A3C+ has slightly higher median and beats A3C significantly on at least a quarter of games.
limits: Median gain small because many games need only epsilon-greedy exploration.
agent_relevance: A count bonus is a niche tool: use it only when plain sampling stalls.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation (appendix, life-loss signal)
finding: A small setup detail mattered: treating loss of a life as episode end was harmful in Montezuma's Revenge.
numbers: Appendix C.3 states the life-loss signal is detrimental in Montezuma's Revenge, though used elsewhere.
limits: Implementation details affect the famous result.
agent_relevance: What counts as a fresh attempt (reset or not) can swing exploration outcomes; define it in code.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models
finding: Replaced CTS with a PixelCNN density model. The pseudo-count idea holds and several original assumptions are not needed.
numbers: DQN-PixelCNN beats DQN-CTS across 57 Atari games. Raising bonus scale 1 to 2 orders of magnitude gave best-run peaks: 900 Gravitar, 6600 Montezuma, 39000 Private Eye, 1500 Venture (5 seeds per scale).
limits: Aggressive scale speeds exploration but hurts stability and long-term score. Peak scores are best runs, not means.
agent_relevance: Bonus strength is a dial: too high spends effort on novelty instead of payoff.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models (Monte Carlo ablation)
finding: The mixed Monte Carlo return matters as much as the bonus. In the hardest games neither alone helps; together they give rapid progress.
numbers: Baseline DQN makes no training progress on the hardest sparse games; neither MMC nor the bonus alone gives significant benefit; the combination does.
limits: Shows the original claim was a package effect.
agent_relevance: A novelty mark must be tied to a fast way to score and propagate it. In the schema, link a rare-direction mark to a quick check.

source: Tang et al. (2017) #Exploration: a study of count-based exploration for deep RL
finding: Simple SimHash counts on states reach near state-of-the-art on deep RL benchmarks. Hash granularity and task-relevant content decide success.
numbers: Atari, TRPO, 50M steps: Freeway 16.5 baseline to 31.6 with pixel-SimHash; Frostbite 2869 baseline to 4683 with pixel-SimHash.
limits: Table text partly garbled on extraction, so only cells that are clear are recorded. Gains uneven across games.
agent_relevance: Counting needs the right state key. For S3, the key for 'same direction' must be neither too fine nor too coarse.

source: Tang et al. (2017) #Exploration: a study of count-based exploration for deep RL (learned hash and key choice)
finding: Better keys help hard games: BASS-SimHash beats pixel-SimHash on Montezuma and Venture, and the learned autoencoder code is much better on Gravitar, Montezuma and Venture.
numbers: Text: TRPO-AE-SimHash achieves near state-of-the-art on Freeway, Frostbite, Solaris. Appendix: too fine a pixel code on Frostbite makes the agent treat every state as new.
limits: Per-game results; no significance tests reported in text read.
agent_relevance: Too fine a key makes every attempt look new; too coarse merges distinct attempts. Choose the key by task.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by random network distillation
finding: RND, a prediction-error novelty bonus that acts like a soft count, finds more rooms than pseudo-counts and sets state of the art on Montezuma.
numbers: Intrinsic-only agent finds over half the rooms; best agent often finds 22 of 24. Final mean: Montezuma RND 8152 vs PPO 2497 vs dynamics 400; Venture 1859 vs 0 dynamics; Private Eye 8666 vs 105 dynamics; Gravitar 3906 vs PPO 3426; Pitfall -3 (fails).
limits: Footnote: with 10 seeds the best CNN setting differed greatly from 5-seed results; Montezuma outcomes dominated by discrete choices (left or right from the first room) and outliers.
agent_relevance: Count-like novelty has high run-to-run variance. Do not trust one run of an exploration policy.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by random network distillation (noisy TV)
finding: A forward-dynamics-error bonus stalls on unpredictable states. Same agent with a dynamics target does much worse on three games.
numbers: Dynamics-based agent significantly worse than RND with same CNN policy on Montezuma, Private Eye, Solaris; similar on Venture, Pitfall, Gravitar. Agent oscillates between two rooms because sticky actions make prediction error irreducible.
quote: This is a manifestation of the 'noisy TV' problem
limits: Only Atari with sticky actions.
agent_relevance: Rarity by what was tried, not by how surprising the model's output is. Surprise over noisy text is a trap.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-scale study of curiosity-driven learning
finding: Purely curiosity-driven agents do well on many games across 54 environments. Random features suffice for many, learned features generalise better.
numbers: 54 environments including Atari. A noisy TV added to a Unity maze drastically slows learning, though agents sometimes still reach the extrinsic reward if run long enough.
limits: Alignment with game score is game specific (e.g. Breakout: agent seeks long episodes).
agent_relevance: Novelty alone approximates task progress only when the task has built-in progress structure.

source: Taiga et al. (2019) On bonus-based exploration methods in the Arcade Learning Environment
finding: Controlled comparison (Rainbow base, same tuning protocol, 5 seeds): bonuses help on Montezuma but not on other hard-exploration games, and epsilon-greedy stays competitive.
numbers: Montezuma performance does not correlate with other hard-exploration games. Epsilon-greedy even beats other methods by a significant margin on Gravitar. On the easy Atari training set pseudo-count is worse on every game except Seaquest; RND and ICM only match epsilon-greedy; NoisyNets most consistent.
quote: bonus-based methods are generally detrimental in the context of easy exploration problems
limits: Hyperparameters tuned only on Montezuma. Only Atari and one base agent.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: a novelty bonus costs performance when exploration is not the problem. Gate it behind a stall check, not always on.

source: Taiga et al. (2019) On bonus-based exploration methods in the Arcade Learning Environment (confounds)
finding: Paper argues exploration papers confound gains with longer training, bigger models and new hyperparameters; earlier claims may reflect better RL algorithms rather than better exploration.
numbers: Protocol: Rainbow with CTS, PixelCNN, RND, ICM, NoisyNets, epsilon-greedy; training curves averaged over 5 seeds; 200M frames.
limits: Argument partly interpretive.
agent_relevance: Compare any novelty bonus against a plain re-sample baseline with equal compute.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2021) First return, then explore (Go-Explore)
finding: Go-Explore keeps an archive of visited cells, returns to a promising one, then explores. It far exceeds intrinsic-motivation agents on Montezuma and Pitfall.
numbers: Montezuma without domain knowledge mean 43,763 (almost 4 times previous best); with domain knowledge mean over 650,000, max 18 million. Pitfall with domain knowledge mean almost 60,000.
limits: Relies on simulator reset (return step) and a later imitation phase. Not a like-for-like RL comparison. Low visit counts favour cell selection.
agent_relevance: Matches S3: an archive of tried directions, return to one, then branch; counts decide which to expand.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Never Give Up: learning directed exploration strategies
finding: Combines within-episode novelty (nearest-neighbour memory) with a lifelong RND factor. Doubles the base agent on hard-exploration games and keeps scores on others.
numbers: Median human-normalised score 1344% on Atari-57. Pitfall mean 8,400 without demonstrations. Table 1: NGU(N=32) Montezuma 10.4k, Pitfall 8.4k, Private Eye 100.0k, Venture 1.7k.
limits: Lifelong term not always helpful: NGU(N=1)-RND scored Montezuma 3.0k vs NGU(N=1) 8.7k, and Venture 46.4 vs 876.3.
agent_relevance: Two timescales of novelty: within one problem and across problems. Keep a per-problem tried-list and test the cross-problem one separately.

source: Martin et al. (2017) Count-based exploration in feature space for RL
finding: Proposes counts computed in a learned feature space (phi-pseudocount) so optimism works with function approximation.
numbers: Numbers not recorded; only abstract and introduction text skimmed.
limits: Not read in depth.
agent_relevance: Generalising counts across similar states is the central design issue, same as grouping similar directions in S3.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Count Counts: MERCI, count-based intrinsic rewards for LLM reasoning
finding: First direct use of learned pseudo-counts (Coin Flipping Network) on LLM reasoning trajectories in RLVR. Small, consistent gains on math and SQL.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B mean@k average: GRPO 40.5 to 42.2 with MERCI; DAPO 42.2 to 44.9. pass@k average GRPO 65.8 to 67.4. AIME25 pass@256 GRPO 50.0 to 60.0; AIME24 76.7 to 80.0. AIME25 mean@256 GRPO 11.2 to 13.4.
limits: Training-time method, not an inference scaffold. Average gains are 1.6 to 2.7 points. Single seed reporting not stated.
agent_relevance: Count-style novelty helps modestly when applied to whole reasoning trajectories; effect small compared with variance.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Count Counts: MERCI, count-based intrinsic rewards for LLM reasoning (ablation)
finding: The bonus needs noise filtering and budget control; without them it can fall below the baseline. Authors say a dense indiscriminate bonus causes unstable aimless exploration.
numbers: GRPO baseline pass@k average 65.8; MERCI 67.4; without noise filtering 63.8; without percentile and spatial filtering 65.6. mean@k average: baseline 40.5, MERCI 42.2, no noise filtering 38.9.
limits: Math task and vanilla GRPO only.
agent_relevance: Bound and filter novelty effort; unbounded novelty seeking lowers accuracy. Supports a cap on exploration steps.

source: Dai et al. (2025) CDE: curiosity-driven exploration for efficient RL in LLMs
finding: Authors tried SimHash pseudo-counts on chain-of-thought embeddings first and report it fails: most responses fall in the same or neighbouring hash cells, so counts are concentrated and uninformative.
numbers: Replacement perplexity bonus: Qwen3-4B-Base GRPO overall average 48.2 to 50.6; AIME24 Avg@16 20.8 to 23.3, Pass@16 41.9 to 48.5. Multi-head PPO critic-variance bonus about +2 average and about +10 Pass@16 on AIME in many cases; gains plateau at 4 or more heads.
quote: most responses collapse into the same or neighboring hash grids
limits: The failed count version appears only as a preliminary figure, not a table.
agent_relevance: Failed transfer to text: counting over embeddings of long reasoning collapses. Count labelled tried directions instead.

source: Dai et al. (2025) CDE: curiosity-driven exploration for efficient RL in LLMs (calibration collapse)
finding: Under naive GRPO the model's confidence decouples from correctness; a perplexity bonus reduces this.
numbers: Reported across AIME25, AIME24, AMC23, MATH; about +3 points on AIME.
limits: Mechanism is the authors' analysis.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model's own confidence on a path it keeps repeating.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Think longer to explore deeper (LIE)
finding: Frames in-context reasoning as state coverage and uses count-based UCB theory to argue exploration needs longer traces. A length reward plus redundancy penalty improves reasoning.
numbers: Average improvement 4.4% in-domain and 2.7% out-of-domain across Qwen3 and Llama models.
limits: Counting is motivation, not an explicit visit count. Gain comes from trace length plus a redundancy penalty.
agent_relevance: A redundancy penalty on repeated attempts is a count-like control: penalise a direction already tried.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does RL really incentivize reasoning capacity beyond the base model?
finding: Standard RLVR narrows rather than widens the set of problems solved at large k, evidence that exploration in LLM RL is weak.
numbers: RL model nearly 30% higher than base at k=1 but eventually surpassed by base. Minerva 32B: base beats RL by about 9% at k=128. Training pass@1 rises 26.1 to 42.5 while pass@256 falls. Rollouts per prompt 8 to 32 does not fix it. KL term gives similar pass@1 but lower pass@128.
limits: Does not test count bonuses directly. Whether scaling RL closes the gap is left open.
agent_relevance: Wide sampling of the base model beats trained policies at large k, so a scaffold that forces diverse attempts uses capacity the policy hides.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does RL really incentivize reasoning capacity beyond the base model? (entropy)
finding: Lower entropy contributes to the narrowing but does not fully explain it; six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and stay far from the base-model upper bound.
numbers: Text: reduced entropy alone does not fully account for the reduction in reasoning boundary.
limits: Competing explanations unresolved.
agent_relevance: Entropy bonuses and count bonuses are not interchangeable; test each.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding pretraining in RL with large language models (ELLM)
finding: Novelty rewards (RND, APT, a Novelty baseline) waste effort in large environments because most novelty is irrelevant. LLM-suggested goals give better-aligned coverage.
numbers: In three of four Housekeep tasks ELLM gives higher pretraining success than RND, APT and Novelty baselines, much higher in the first two tasks where LLM goal accuracy (Table 3) is higher.
limits: Gain scales with how accurate the LLM goals are. Crafter numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Weight rarity by relevance. Let the model propose which untried directions are plausible; let code count them.

source: Auer (2002) UCB bound as stated in Wang et al. (2026), Theorem 3.1
finding: Count-based UCB is regret-optimal in bandits.
numbers: Regret limit at most 8 log T times the sum over suboptimal actions of 1/gap, as stated in the LIE paper.
limits: Theory is for bandits; real and language settings lack clean counts.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule: try each direction in proportion to uncertainty, stop once the gap is known.

source: Taiga et al. (2019), tuning on one game
finding: Tuning on one flagship game gives results that do not transfer.
numbers: Montezuma results do not correlate with other hard-exploration games; method gaps are smaller elsewhere.
limits: Whole field tuned on Montezuma.
agent_relevance: Do not tune the novelty weight on the same benchmark you report.
